text.p: The leader of the Philippine Senate was ousted on Thursday as opposition legislators closed ranks against efforts to change the constitution and extend President Fidel Ramos's term of office.

Ramos, who has repeatedly expressed his commitment to stepping down when his term expires in 1998, said in a statement he was confident the sacking of Senator Neptali Gonzales would not jeopardise the country's recent economic progress.
Gonzales, who had been Senate president for more than a year, was replaced by veteran politician Ernesto Maceda, who had orchestrated the move against him.
Maceda told a news conference he would "absolutely and unconditionally" oppose moves to amend the constitution that have been gathering strength within Ramos's Lakas party.

Despite Ramos's stated objections, Lakas party workers are gathering signatures for a national petition that would pave the way for a constitutional change allowing the head of state more than the six-year term currently permitted by law.
Maceda also said the removal of Gonzales would strengthen unity among fragmented opposition parties.
"This development will change the political landscape. There will be a bigger opposition in the Congress," he said.

Maceda's motion for the removal of Gonzales was signed by 14 other members of the 24-member chamber. The move was also supported by Edgardo Angara, who was himself ousted as Senate president last August.
"This is a turning point in our political life. We thank President Ramos for providing the causus belli for this unification," Angara told a news conference.
"If not for the revival of moves for charter changes, the opposition would have remained fragmented," he added.
Gonzales shrugged off his removal as par for the course in Philippine politics, which is marked by fluid loyalties and endless horse-trading.
"It's a game of musical chairs," he told reporters. "I've been in this game for a long time. I know how it works."
In a statement, Ramos extended his congratulations to Maceda and added: "... I am confident that this development will not set back the gains our country has achieved so far."
Lakas party members occupy just four Senate seats, the rest being divided among three other parties and independents.
Ramos has, however, been able to forge a sufficient degree of consensus to allow passage of a wide range of economic reforms since he took office in 1992.
